text: 🇲🇽🌎 "Only the people of Mexico can decide their destiny — no foreign power, no elite." Recalling Morelos and the Sentimientos de la Nación, Sheinbaum returned to the root of independence: "Sovereignty springs from the people." — President Claudia Sheinbaum, Hidalgo Pachuca, Sept 13, 2026 — the month of the patria, marking 216 years since Hidalgo's call to independence.
📸 Niños Héroes de Chapultepec — 13 de septiembre de 2026, Ciudad de México

🇲🇽🌎 179 years ago, teenage cadets chose death over surrender to a U.S. invasion. Today Mexico honored them. President Claudia Sheinbaum led the commemoration of the Gesta Heroica de Chapultepec — six cadets and two officers of the Colegio Militar who fell defending the castle against the invading U.S. Army in 1847. — 179th Anniversary of the Niños Héroes, Altar a la Patria, Mexico City

🇲🇽⚖️ "The homeland is honored, independence is preserved, and sovereignty is defended." On the 179th anniversary of the U.S. invasion of Mexico, the message from the Altar a la Patria was one line. — Gen. Ricardo Trevilla, Defense Secretary, Mexico City He called that sovereignty — the one the cadets died defending in 1847 — not merely a historical aspiration, but a constitutional mandate.

🇲🇽🌎 The U.S. general who invaded Mexico admitted it — in his own memoirs. "The Mexicans have shown a patriotism we would do well to imitate." — Gen. Ricardo Trevilla, Defense Secretary, quoting Ulysses S. Grant 179 years after the U.S. invasion of 1846–47, Mexico honored the teenage cadets who defended Chapultepec to the death. Grant — a young officer in that war, later U.S. president — wrote those words about the enemy he fought.

🇲🇽🏭 Mexico's aim in the U.S. trade talks: strike down the tariffs it calls unjust. President Sheinbaum said the goal is to lift U.S. duties on steel, aluminum and automobiles — which she calls unjust and harmful — and to block a new round Washington has floated under an "overcapacity" argument. — Claudia Sheinbaum, on trade negotiations with the U.S.

🇲🇽🌎 "We will not sign anything that harms our sovereignty or our economy." Ahead of trade talks with Washington, President Sheinbaum set Mexico's red line for the T-MEC review: sovereignty and the national economy are not on the table. — Claudia Sheinbaum, on the T-MEC renegotiation with the U.S. She said most of the 54 disputed points are already resolved, and that Mexico will keep defending the trilateral agreement.

🇲🇽💵 <u>PESO SHRUGS OFF TRUMP'S TARIFF THREATS — 8TH DAY UNDER 17</u>

Fresh protectionist noise from Washington and a T-MEC renegotiation grinding through its fourth round in DC, and the peso still closed Friday near 16.97 to the dollar — its eighth straight session under 17. El Financiero flagged the "risk aversion" from Trump's new tariff threats; the currency barely flinched, slipping less than half a percent on the week while holding one of its strongest levels of the year.

🚨🇲🇽 <u>"NO ELITE, NO FOREIGN GOVERNMENT WILL DECIDE MEXICO'S FUTURE"</u>

As Washington leans on Mexico in the T-MEC renegotiation and Marco Rubio claims cartels still control stretches of the country, Sheinbaum drew the line from Veracruz: "Sovereignty emanates from the people. Only the Mexican people can define their present and their future — no elite, no foreign government." Her limit in the trade talks, she said, is "sovereignty and that which we consider should not be negotiable."

🇲🇽🌎 <u>NO SECOND PASSPORT FOR MEXICO'S PRESIDENT OR GOVERNORS</u>

A constitutional reform requiring single Mexican nationality for the president, state governors and the CDMX head of government has cleared committee. Sheinbaum's logic is blunt: Mexican ambassadors already can't hold a second passport, so neither should whoever commands the country. "There are two parties that openly voted against it," she noted — the PRI and Movimiento Ciudadano — while the PAN abstained. Ordinary citizens keep their dual nationality; this touches only those who hold ultimate power.
